types.name: Control
types.desc: Calls that carry no payload or only names: requests, checks, refusals, unmounts, sync-task dispatch. Drawn dashed.

types.name: Transaction
types.desc: A sync task joining the open txg, a txg being synced, or a wait for a txg.

types.name: Block pointer
types.desc: Blocks of a destroyed dataset handed to the freeing machinery: deadlist sub-lists, a root block pointer, livelist entries.

types.name: Configuration and properties
types.desc: Pool configuration: the pool state written into the labels, the cache file entry, label contents read at import.

contexts.name: Kernel, in the thread of the calling process (an ioctl on /dev/zfs, mount(2) or umount(2)) or a helper thread it starts, outside syncing context and outside any dmu_tx
Syncing context: txg_sync thread or dp_sync_taskq workers, one txg at a time
A dedicated kernel thread or zthr
Runs in whichever context calls it

groups.title: Userspace: zfs(8), zpool(8), libzfs
groups.summary: Decide what to destroy and in which order, refuse children and clones, unmount, and send the requests.

groups.title: Kernel entry: ioctls, holds, sync tasks
groups.summary: Unmount snapshots, drop volume devices, and run each destroy as a sync task.

groups.title: TXG sync (shared with the I/O graph)
groups.summary: Where the queued destroy tasks run, after the txg's data is written.

groups.title: Destroy checks and sync tasks
groups.summary: Checks that refuse a destroy, and the sync functions that remove the dataset records.

groups.title: Freeing (detail in the snapshot graph)
groups.summary: Where the destroyed blocks wait, and the background work that frees them a slice per txg.

groups.title: Pool destroy
groups.summary: spa_export_common() with POOL_STATE_DESTROYED: the labels, the final txgs and the cache file.

nodes.title: Administrator
nodes.role: The person or script typing the command. Every path in this graph that a command starts begins with a wire from this node; the arrows that come back into a command node are its results, errors and refusals.

nodes.title: zfs(8) command
nodes.role: zfs destroy. A name with @ is a snapshot list, a name with # a bookmark (not drawn), anything else a file system or volume; a pool's root file system is refused without -r. destroy_callback() gets every dataset to destroy in order: a snapshot is added to the current batch, a file system or volume first flushes the batch (destroy_batched()), is unmounted and is then destroyed. With -r an error on one dataset is remembered and the walk goes on.

nodes.title: Snapshot list (fs@a%b, -r)
nodes.role: Expands the part after @: a comma-separated list of names and ranges, where a%b is every snapshot from a to b in creation order and an empty end means the first or the last. With -r the same spec is applied to every descendant file system. Every match goes into one nvlist; a name that matches nothing is skipped silently, and an empty list is an error.

nodes.title: Dependents check and walk (-r, -R)
nodes.role: zfs_iter_dependents_v2() visits a dataset's dependents depth first and calls back after the children: child file systems first, then the snapshots in creation order, and each snapshot only after its clones. destroy_check_dependent() uses the same walk to refuse: children or snapshots without -r, clones without -R.

nodes.title: Dry run and space estimate (-n, -v)
nodes.role: With -v (or -p) for a snapshot list, walks each file system's snapshots in creation order, prints each selected one and asks the kernel how much each contiguous range would free. With -n nothing is destroyed. For a file system, -nv only lists the datasets, without an estimate.

nodes.title: zpool(8) command
nodes.role: zpool destroy [-f] pool: unmount everything, then one ioctl. -f only forces the unmounts. zpool import -D is the way back: it lists and imports only pools whose labels say destroyed.

nodes.title: libzfs / libzfs_core
nodes.role: Turns each request into one ioctl: lzc_destroy_snaps() for a snapshot list (with defer for -d), lzc_destroy() for one file system or volume, ZFS_IOC_POOL_DESTROY for a pool. Translates the errors: EEXIST is "snapshot is cloned", EBUSY with user holds is "it's being held".

nodes.title: libzfs mount / unmount
nodes.role: Unshares (NFS, SMB) and unmounts a file system that /proc/self/mounts lists as mounted; a volume or an unmounted file system needs nothing. If the unmount fails the file system is shared again. After a destroy, remove_mountpoint() deletes the empty mountpoint directory when the mountpoint is default or inherited. For zpool destroy, zpool_disable_datasets() does the same for every mounted file system of the pool.

nodes.title: ZFS ioctl handlers
nodes.role: Kernel entry points. Before a snapshot destroy they unmount the snapshots and remove their volume devices; zfs_ioc_destroy() retries a file system destroy after removing a leftover %recv child; zfs_ioc_space_snaps() answers the dry-run estimate without changing anything.

nodes.title: Space estimate
nodes.role: What destroying the snapshots first to last of one file system would free: for each dataset after a snapshot in the range, the space on its deadlist born after the snapshot before first. Read-only, under a pool hold.

nodes.title: Snapshot automount unmount
nodes.role: A snapshot visited under .zfs/snapshot is automounted. Before it is destroyed it is unmounted, best effort: the kernel invalidates the mount and waits briefly until the snapshot has no long hold.

nodes.title: Kernel unmount (zfs_umount)
nodes.role: umount(2) on a ZFS file system ends in zfs_umount() (from zpl_put_super()). It tears down the zfsvfs and gives up ownership of the objset, which drops the mount's long hold on the dataset.

nodes.title: Dataset long holds
nodes.role: A long hold keeps a dataset from being destroyed while it is in use. Owners take one (a mounted file system, an open volume, a receive), and so do other long operations such as a send. Any long hold makes a destroy fail with EBUSY; only a snapshot whose holder is a mount can be marked with -d instead.

nodes.title: DSL request functions
nodes.role: dsl_destroy_snapshots_nvl() runs one sync task per snapshot, in list order, and stops at the first error, so a failed request can leave the earlier snapshots destroyed. dsl_destroy_head() runs one sync task for the file system or volume (two, with an open-context pre-free in between, on pools without async_destroy).

nodes.title: dsl_sync_task()
nodes.role: Runs a metadata change in syncing context. The check runs once in open context as a quick test, the task is queued on the open txg, and the caller waits until that txg has synced. In syncing context dsl_sync_task_sync() checks pool space and re-runs the check before the sync function. Destroys use ZFS_SPACE_CHECK_DESTROY, which may use three quarters of the slop space, so a nearly full pool can still destroy.

nodes.title: Old-pool pre-free and crash cleanup

ref.code: dmu_object_next(objset_t *os, uint64_t *objectp, boolean_t hole, uint64_t txg)

nodes.role: Only on pools without the async_destroy feature, where the whole tree is freed in the destroy's txg. A first sync task marks the dataset inconsistent; then every object changed since the last snapshot is freed from open context so that the final txg stays short. If the system crashes in between, the next import finds the inconsistent dataset and finishes the destroy (dsl_destroy_inconsistent()), unless it is a resumable receive.

nodes.title: zvol device removal
nodes.role: Removes the /dev/zvol device of a volume, of its snapshots (present only with snapdev=visible) and of everything below a name. zvol_remove_minors() queues the work on the pool's zvol taskq; the destroy paths do not wait for it, zpool destroy does.

nodes.title: TXG: syncing (txg_sync_thread)
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Syncs the txg a destroy task joined. txg_wait_synced() is why zfs destroy returns only when the destroy is on disk, and why zpool destroy can push the final label update out before the pool is unloaded.

nodes.title: spa_sync()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Each pass runs dsl_pool_sync(), which runs the destroy tasks in pass 1; dsl_scan_sync() then frees queued blocks; every txg ends by rewriting the labels and uberblocks.

nodes.title: dsl_pool_sync()
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Writes the txg's dirty datasets first and only then runs the queued sync tasks, so a dataset destroyed in txg N had its last writes synced in the same txg.

nodes.title: Snapshot destroy checks
nodes.role: Runs in open context and again in syncing context. A snapshot that no longer exists passes and is skipped. A long hold refuses with EBUSY, unless -d and the holder is a mount. With -d nothing else is checked (ENOTSUP on pools older than user holds). Without -d, user holds refuse with EBUSY and clones with EEXIST.

nodes.title: Snapshot destroy
nodes.role: Destroys one snapshot record and moves its blocks on (detail: snapshot lifecycle graph, path destroy_snapshot). With -d, while user holds, clones or a long hold remain, it only sets defer_destroy. Afterwards it queues removal of the snapshot's volume device.

nodes.title: User holds
nodes.role: Where a snapshot marked defer_destroy because of user holds is finally destroyed: zfs release of the last hold, on a snapshot with no clones and no long hold, runs the snapshot destroy in the same sync task.

nodes.title: File system destroy checks
nodes.role: Runs in open context and again in syncing context. EBUSY when the dataset has a long hold (still mounted, an open volume, a send) or still has snapshots of its own; EEXIST when it has child datasets. A clone whose deferred origin would be destroyed with it is also refused while that origin snapshot has a long hold.

nodes.title: File system destroy
nodes.role: Destroys a head dataset (file system, volume or clone) in one sync task: drops its deadlist, hands its blocks to the clone livelist, the bptree or (old pools) frees them in this txg, removes the dataset and directory records, and, for a clone whose origin is marked defer_destroy and has no other clone or hold, destroys that origin snapshot too. Then it queues removal of the volume devices.

nodes.title: Deadlist split and merge
nodes.role: Snapshot destroy on the deadlists: the part of the next dataset's deadlist that only the destroyed snapshot referenced is moved to the pool free list, and the destroyed snapshot's own deadlist is merged into the next one. See the snapshot lifecycle graph.

nodes.title: Pool free list (dp_free_bpobj)
nodes.role: The pool-wide list of blocks waiting to be freed in the background. A snapshot destroy only moves whole deadlist sub-lists here, so its txg does no per-block work. Counted in the freeing pool property.

nodes.title: Async-destroy queue (bptree)

ref.code: bptree_add(objset_t *os, uint64_t obj, blkptr_t *bp, uint64_t birth_txg,
bptree_iterate(objset_t *os, uint64_t obj, boolean_t free, bptree_itor_t func,

nodes.role: One entry per destroyed file system or volume: its root block pointer and the txg at or below which blocks still belong to an older snapshot. The background traversal frees the newer blocks.

nodes.title: Livelist delete thread
nodes.role: The z_livelist_destroy zthr. A destroyed clone that kept a livelist is freed from that list, one sub-list at a time, without walking the clone's tree.

nodes.title: dsl_process_async_destroys()
nodes.role: Called from dsl_scan_sync() in sync pass 1 of every txg while frees are pending: first the pool free list, then the bptree. It stops for this txg when its block or time budget is used up, so a large destroy is spread over many txgs and the freeing property counts down.

nodes.title: metaslab_free()

ref.code: metaslab_free(spa_t *spa, const blkptr_t *bp, uint64_t txg, boolean_t now)

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. Records the freed segments in the metaslab. They become allocatable TXG_DEFER_SIZE (2) txgs later.

nodes.title: spa_export_common()
nodes.role: spa_destroy() is spa_export_common() with POOL_STATE_DESTROYED. It suspends async tasks, waits for dirty data and closing datasets, refuses with EBUSY while anything still holds the pool, removes every volume device, stops initialize, trim and rebuild, sets the pool state and marks all labels dirty, then unloads the pool and forgets it. It frees no blocks and overwrites no data.

nodes.title: spa_unload()
nodes.role: Syncs the last txgs (up to the final txg set by spa_export_common()), stops the txg threads, waits for outstanding I/O and frees the in-memory vdev tree.

nodes.title: Pool cache file (zpool.cache)
nodes.role: Rewrites the cache file without the destroyed pool, so it is not imported at boot, and removes the pool from the kernel's namespace.

nodes.title: Uberblock + label update

ref.code: vdev_config_sync(spa_t *spa, vdev_t **svd, int svdcount, uint64_t txg,
spa_config_generate(spa_t *spa, vdev_t *vd, uint64_t txg, int getstats)

nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. The end of every txg. With the configuration marked dirty, the labels of every leaf are rewritten from spa_config_generate(), which records the current pool state; this is how POOL_STATE_DESTROYED reaches the disks.

nodes.title: Labels L0-L3 + uberblock ring
nodes.role: Shared with the I/O flow graph. After zpool destroy the four labels on every leaf still hold the full pool configuration, with pool_state destroyed (2), and the uberblock ring still points at intact data.

wires.label: zfs destroy fs@spec: zfs_do_destroy() calls gather_snapshots(), which expands the spec with zfs_iter_snapspec_v2() and, with -r, repeats it for each descendant file system (zfs_iter_filesystems_v2())
snapshot_to_nvl_cb(): unless -R or -d, zfs_iter_dependents_v2() with destroy_check_dependent() looks for clones of each snapshot before it is added to the list
refused before any ioctl: destroy_check_dependent() prints "has children" (child datasets or snapshots, needs -r) or "has dependent clones" (needs -R) and sets cb_error, and zfs_do_destroy() stops

-v: destroy_print_snapshots() walks the file system's snapshots in creation order (zfs_iter_snapshots_sorted_v2()), prints "would destroy" or "will destroy" and groups the selected ones into contiguous ranges
for each range: lzc_snaprange_space(first, last) -> ZFS_IOC_SPACE_SNAPS -> zfs_ioc_space_snaps()
zfs_ioc_space_snaps() takes a pool hold (dsl_pool_hold()), not a sync task, and calls dsl_dataset_space_wouldfree(first, last)
from the snapshot after last back to the one after first (ds_next_snap_obj), dsl_deadlist_space_range() sums the deadlist space born after first's ds_prev_snap_txg; the ranges add up in cb_snapused
zfs_do_destroy() prints "would reclaim" (-n) or "will reclaim"; with -n (cb_dryrun) it stops here and sends no destroy request
zfs_destroy_snaps_nvl(cb_nvl, defer): every gathered snapshot, of every file system with -r, in one request; lzc_destroy_snaps() adds "defer" for -d
lzc_destroy_snaps(): ZFS_IOC_DESTROY_SNAPS -> zfs_ioc_destroy_snaps()
for each name: EXDEV if it is not in this pool; zfs_unmount_snap() -> zfsctl_snapshot_unmount() unmounts an automounted .zfs/snapshot mount

zfsctl_snapshot_unmount_wait() waits up to about 40 ms (MSEC_TO_TICK(40)) for the snapshot to lose its long hold (dsl_dataset_long_held()); if it is still busy the destroy goes on and the check decides
zvol_remove_minors(spa, snapshot, async): the snapshot's volume device, if any, is removed on the zvol taskq (taskq_dispatch())
zfs_ioc_destroy_snaps() -> dsl_destroy_snapshots_nvl(snaps, defer, errlist)
one dsl_sync_task(dsl_destroy_snapshot_check, dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync) per snapshot, with ZFS_SPACE_CHECK_DESTROY; the first error is put in errlist (fnvlist_add_int32()) and ends the loop
dsl_sync_task_common(): the check runs first in open context (dst_checkfunc, pool config lock as reader); an error returns at once, before any txg

refused: user holds (ds_userrefs > 0) give EBUSY, clones (ds_num_children > 1) EEXIST; the error comes back in errlist (fnvlist_add_int32()) and zfs_destroy_snaps_nvl() prints "snapshot is cloned" or, after lzc_get_holds(), "it's being held"
dmu_tx_assign() joins the open txg, the task is queued on dp_sync_tasks (txg_list_add_tail()), and txg_wait_synced() sleeps until that txg is on disk
txg_sync_thread() -> spa_sync(txg)
spa_sync_iterate_to_convergence(): dsl_pool_sync() in every pass
sync pass 1, after the dirty datasets are written: dsl_sync_task_sync() checks pool space (ENOSPC) and re-runs dsl_destroy_snapshot_check() (dst_checkfunc) with the config lock held as writer
dsl_destroy_snapshot_check_impl(): a long hold (dsl_dataset_long_held()) refuses with EBUSY, unless -d and the holder is a mount (dsl_dataset_has_owner())
the check passed: dst_syncfunc -> dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync() -> dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync_impl()

-d while user holds (ds_userrefs), clones (ds_num_children > 1) or a long hold remain: only DS_FLAG_DEFER_DESTROY is set and nothing is freed; a mount that lets go triggers a later sweep (SPA_ASYNC_DEFER_DESTROY), the last release destroys it in its own sync task

dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync_impl(): the next dataset's deadlist is split at this snapshot's previous-snapshot txg (dsl_deadlist_move_bpobj()) and this snapshot's deadlist is merged into it (dsl_deadlist_merge())
blocks only this snapshot referenced move whole to the pool free list (bpobj_enqueue_subobj()); freeing grows (dp_free_dir)
dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync(): zvol_remove_minors(snapshot name, async) after the record is gone
in the next txgs: spa_sync_iterate_to_convergence() -> dsl_scan_sync(), which calls dsl_process_async_destroys() while frees are pending
bpobj_iterate(dp_free_bpobj): entries are freed and removed from the list
dsl_scan_free_block_cb() -> zio_free_sync() -> metaslab_free() for an ordinary block, and freeing shrinks (dp_free_dir); gang, dedup and cloned blocks take a free zio (snapshot graph)

dsl_scan_async_block_should_pause(): past zfs_async_block_max_blocks, or past zfs_free_min_time_ms (scn_async_block_min_time_ms) while a sync is waiting, it returns ERESTART and the rest waits for the next txg
zfs destroy fs: unless -R, zfs_iter_dependents_v2() with destroy_check_dependent() checks for children and snapshots (allowed with -r) and for clones outside the tree (allowed with -R)

zfs_iter_dependents_v2(target, destroy_callback) walks every dependent depth first: child file systems (zfs_iter_filesystems_v2()), then snapshots in creation order (zfs_iter_snapshots_sorted_v2()), each after its clones (zfs_iter_clones()); for fs@snap -R, destroy_clones() does the same for each snapshot
iter_dependents_cb() calls destroy_callback() for each dependent after its own dependents; zfs_do_destroy() then calls destroy_callback() for the target itself
destroy_callback(): a snapshot is only added to cb_batchedsnaps; a file system first flushes the batch, destroy_batched() -> zfs_destroy_snaps_nvl()
destroy_callback() -> zfs_unmount(dataset, MS_FORCE with -f): if it is mounted (libzfs_mnttab_find()), zfs_unshare() and zfs_commit_shares(), then unmount_one()
do_unmount(): umount2(mountpoint, flags), or /bin/umount when ZFS_MOUNT_HELPER is set; the kernel ends in zpl_put_super() -> zfs_umount()
zfs_umount(): zfsvfs_teardown(), then dmu_objset_disown() -> dsl_dataset_disown() -> dsl_dataset_long_rele(): the mount's long hold is gone

the unmount fails (EBUSY: a file open or a working directory inside, without -f): unmount_one() reports "cannot unmount", zfs_share() shares it again, nothing is destroyed; with -r cb_error is set and the walk continues
zfs_destroy(dataset, no defer) -> lzc_destroy(name)
lzc_destroy(): ZFS_IOC_DESTROY -> zfs_ioc_destroy()
zfs_ioc_destroy() -> dsl_destroy_head(name); on EEXIST it destroys a hidden child name/%recv (recv_clone_name) left by an interrupted receive and tries again

dsl_destroy_head() -> zfs_destroy_unmount_origin(): for a clone whose origin snapshot is marked defer_destroy (DS_IS_DEFER_DESTROY()), that origin is unmounted (zfs_unmount_snap()), since it may be destroyed with the clone

pool without async_destroy: a first sync task (dsl_destroy_head_begin_sync()) sets DS_FLAG_INCONSISTENT; then dmu_free_long_object() frees each object changed since the last snapshot from open context and txg_wait_synced() pushes the frees out
dsl_sync_task(dsl_destroy_head_check, dsl_destroy_head_sync, ZFS_SPACE_CHECK_DESTROY)
dsl_sync_task_common(): dsl_destroy_head_check() runs first in open context (dst_checkfunc); an error returns at once, before any txg
sync pass 1: dsl_sync_task_sync() checks pool space and re-runs dsl_destroy_head_check() (dst_checkfunc) with the config lock held as writer
dsl_destroy_head_check_impl(): the long hold count (ds_longholds) must be zero; a mount that is still there or an open volume gives EBUSY
refused: EBUSY for a long hold or for snapshots of its own (ds_next_snap_obj), EEXIST for child datasets (dd_child_dir_zapobj); zfs_destroy() prints "cannot destroy"
the check passed: dst_syncfunc -> dsl_destroy_head_sync() -> dsl_destroy_head_sync_impl()
async_destroy enabled (normal): dsl_async_dataset_destroy() -> bptree_add(root block pointer, ds_prev_snap_txg); the dataset's space moves to freeing (dp_free_dir)
a clone with an open livelist: dsl_async_clone_destroy() adds the livelist to the pool's deleted-clones ZAP (zap_add_int()) and wakes the delete thread (zthr_wakeup())
pool without async_destroy: old_synchronous_dataset_destroy() -> traverse_dataset() -> kill_blkptr() -> dsl_dataset_block_kill() frees every block born after ds_prev_snap_txg in this txg
dsl_destroy_head_sync(): zvol_remove_minors(name, async): the volume's device and those of its snapshots go away
rmorigin: the clone's origin is marked defer_destroy, has no user holds and no other clone, so dsl_destroy_snapshot_sync_impl() destroys it in the same sync task
after the free list: bptree_iterate() -> traverse_dataset_destroyed() frees the blocks born after each entry's txg, a slice per txg
spa_livelist_delete_cb(): dsl_process_sub_livelist() keeps the ALLOC entries of one sub-list without a matching FREE, and a sync task (dsl_sync_task()) frees them (zio_free())
zfs_destroy() succeeded: remove_mountpoint() removes the mountpoint directory (rmdir()) if the mountpoint is default or inherited (ZPROP_SRC_DEFAULT)

zpool destroy [-f]: zpool_disable_datasets() reads the mount table (getmntent()), unshares every file system of the pool (unshare_one()), unmounts them in reverse mountpoint order, children first (qsort(), unmount_one()), and removes their mountpoint directories
an unmount fails: "could not unmount datasets", the pool is left as it was
zpool_destroy(pool, history): ZFS_IOC_POOL_DESTROY
ZFS_IOC_POOL_DESTROY -> zfs_ioc_pool_destroy(): zfs_log_history() records the command, then spa_destroy()
spa_destroy() -> spa_export_common(pool, POOL_STATE_DESTROYED, no force, no hardforce)
spa_async_suspend(); txg_wait_synced() so dirty objsets close, and spa_evicting_os_wait() for datasets still being evicted
spa_refcount_zero() is false: something still holds the pool (an open volume takes spa_open_ref(), so does every held dataset directory), EBUSY, the pool stays imported
zvol_remove_minors(pool, async) and taskq_wait(): every volume device of the pool is gone before the pool is unloaded

vdev_initialize_stop_all() and the other stops, then spa_state = new_state (POOL_STATE_DESTROYED) and vdev_config_dirty(root vdev), so the next txgs rewrite every label; spa_final_txg = last synced txg + TXG_DEFER_SIZE + 1
sysevent ESC_ZFS_POOL_DESTROY, then spa_unload() and spa_deactivate()
txg_sync_stop(): txg_wait_synced(open txg + TXG_DEFER_SIZE) syncs the final txgs, then the sync threads exit
every txg ends in spa_sync_rewrite_vdev_config(); with the config dirty (spa_config_dirty_list), vdev_config_sync() writes the labels of all top-level vdevs
vdev_label_sync(): the label nvlist from spa_config_generate() carries ZPOOL_CONFIG_POOL_STATE = destroyed; vdev_label_write() writes it to the label copies; the data is not touched
spa_write_cachefile(removing): the pool's entry is left out of zpool.cache, then spa_remove() drops the pool from the namespace
zpool_destroy() succeeded: remove_mountpoint() of the pool's root file system
later, zpool import -D (do_destroyed): import_pools() keeps only pools whose label pool_state is POOL_STATE_DESTROYED; one last used by another host needs -f (zfs_force_import_required())
runs zfs destroy [-r] [-R] [-f] [-d] [-n] [-v] on a snapshot, snapshot range, file system or volume
runs zpool destroy [-f] pool

paths.title: Destroy one snapshot
paths.summary: zfs destroy pool/fs@snap, from the command line to the sync task that removes the record, and on to the background freeing that returns its unique space. The block-level detail is in `zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:destroy_snapshot`.
paths.ends: The snapshot is gone when the command returns. Its unique blocks are freed in the following txgs (see `zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:free_drain`); the pool property freeing shows what is left, and the space is allocatable two txgs after it is freed.

steps.note: no clones: the snapshot goes into the list
large frees continue over several txgs

paths.title: Snapshot range or -r: one request, one sync task per snapshot
paths.summary: zfs destroy -r pool/fs@a%c collects every matching snapshot of fs and its descendants into one nvlist and one ioctl. The kernel still destroys them one sync task at a time, each waiting for its txg, so the request is not atomic: if a later snapshot is refused, the earlier ones stay destroyed.
paths.ends: With `ok` every snapshot is gone, one txg each, and their blocks wait on the pool free list (`zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:free_drain`). With `fail` the command reports the held snapshot, and the snapshots before it in the list are destroyed.

options.label: The second snapshot has a user hold

steps.note: with -r the spec is applied to every descendant
snapshot 2: a new sync task, after snapshot 1's txg is on disk
snapshot 1 is already destroyed; the rest of the list is not tried
and so on for each further snapshot

paths.title: Refused: a clone or a hold, and -d instead
paths.summary: Why a snapshot destroy is refused, and what -d does instead. A clone is caught by zfs(8) before any request is sent; a user hold is caught by the kernel's open-context check, before any txg; with -d both checks are skipped and the snapshot is only marked.
paths.ends: With `clone` and `hold` nothing has changed. With `defer` the snapshot stays, marked defer_destroy; it is destroyed by the last zfs release (`zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:holds_defer`) or together with its last clone (path defer_clone).

options.label: The snapshot has a user hold
zfs destroy -d on a held or cloned snapshot

steps.note: EBUSY: run zfs holds -r to see the tags
with -d holds and clones are not checked

paths.title: Dry run with space estimate (zfs destroy -nv)
paths.summary: zfs destroy -nv pool/fs@a%c lists what would be destroyed and how much space that would free, without changing anything.
paths.ends: Nothing has changed. The estimate is what destroying exactly these snapshots would free at this moment; blocks also held by snapshots outside the list are not counted, and a later destroy of those snapshots can free more. Without -n, -v prints the same and then destroys (path destroy_batch).

paths.title: Destroy a file system or a volume
paths.summary: zfs destroy pool/fs, for a file system or volume without children or snapshots: the dependency check, the unmount, one sync task, and the background freeing. The block-level detail is in `zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:destroy_filesystem`.
paths.ends: The dataset is gone after one txg (two, plus the pre-free, on old pools). With async_destroy its blocks come back over the following txgs while freeing counts down.

steps.note: no dependents: only the target itself
no mount and no open volume left
the whole tree in this one txg

paths.title: Refused: children, clones or busy
paths.summary: The reasons zfs destroy pool/fs stops. Children, snapshots and outside clones are found by zfs(8) before anything changes; a file system in use fails to unmount; a volume that is open (or any other long hold) is refused by the kernel check.
paths.ends: Nothing is destroyed. Close the files or the volume, or use -r, -R or -f as the message says.

options.label: Has child datasets or snapshots, no -r
-r, but a snapshot has a clone outside the tree

steps.note: the message says use -r or use -R and lists the datasets
a volume has nothing to unmount
the open volume owns the dataset

paths.title: zfs destroy -R: descendants and clones, in order
paths.summary: zfs destroy -R pool/fs, where fs has a snapshot fs@s1 that is the origin of a clone pool/c elsewhere in the pool. zfs(8) destroys the clone first, then the batched snapshot, then fs itself. Each file system or volume is its own ioctl and its own txg.
paths.ends: The clone, the snapshot and the file system are gone, in three requests and at least three txgs. Their blocks are freed in the background from the livelist, the pool free list and the bptree (`zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:destroy_filesystem`). With -r instead of -R the same command is refused, because the clone is outside pool/fs (path fs_refused).

steps.note: first the clone pool/c, reached through fs@s1
then fs@s1, which only joins the batch; then the target fs
the batch is sent before fs is unmounted

paths.title: zfs destroy -d on a cloned snapshot, then destroy the clone
paths.summary: zfs destroy -d pool/fs@s1 while pool/c is a clone of it only marks the snapshot. Destroying the clone later takes the marked origin with it, in the same sync task.
paths.ends: The clone and its origin snapshot are both gone after one txg; their blocks are freed in the background (`zfs-snapshot-lifecycle:free_drain`).

steps.note: the clone keeps it: only marked
the marked origin may go too

paths.title: zpool destroy, and the way back with import -D
paths.summary: zpool destroy pool: every file system is unmounted, the kernel marks the pool destroyed in every label, syncs the final txgs and forgets the pool. No block is freed. zpool import -D can find it again later.
paths.ends: With `ok` the pool is gone from the system and from zpool.cache, but every disk still carries a complete pool marked destroyed. Creating a new pool on the disks or zpool labelclear makes that permanent. With `busy` or `held` the pool is still imported (its file systems may be partly unmounted with `held`).

options.label: A file system cannot be unmounted
A volume of the pool is open

steps.note: an open volume is not closed for you
the pool comes back with its data

model: `zfs destroy` is mostly a userspace program. zfs(8) works out what to destroy and in which order, refuses children and clones itself before anything changes, and unmounts file systems. The kernel destroys one file system or volume per call, or a list of snapshots, and refuses only what it can see: user holds, clones and datasets still in use.

The order is post-order: descendants before their parent, a snapshot's clones before the snapshot, a file system's snapshots before the file system. Contiguous snapshots are batched into one request, and the batch is sent before the next file system is unmounted and destroyed.

A list of snapshots is one ioctl but not one transaction. The kernel runs one sync task per snapshot, each waiting for its own txg; the first refusal stops the list, and the snapshots before it stay destroyed.

"Busy" means a long hold on the dataset: a mount, an open volume, a running send. A mounted file system is unmounted by zfs(8) first (`-f` forces it); an open volume is not closed for you. `zfs destroy -d` turns a refusal caused by holds, clones or a snapshot mount into a mark (`defer_destroy`), and the snapshot goes when the last of them does.

The command returns once the destroy is on disk, but the space returns later. A snapshot's unique blocks go to the pool free list, a file system's tree to the bptree and a clone's blocks to its livelist; `dsl_scan_sync()` frees a time-limited slice of them each txg (pool property `freeing`), and freed space is reusable TXG_DEFER_SIZE (2) txgs later.

`zpool destroy` frees nothing. It unmounts every file system, refuses while anything still holds the pool, writes `POOL_STATE_DESTROYED` into every label, unloads the pool and drops it from the cache file. The data stays on the disks, and `zpool import -D` can bring the pool back until they are reused.
simplifications: The block-level freeing is summarised in one column. Deadlist splitting, bptree traversal, livelists, free zios for gang, dedup and cloned blocks, and space accounting are drawn in the snapshot lifecycle graph.
Recursive destroys are drawn with one clone and one snapshot. Real walks repeat the same steps per dataset; with -r an error on one dataset is reported and the walk continues.

The deferred-destroy sweep after a mounted snapshot is unmounted (`dsl_destroy_snapshot_deferred()` on the async thread) and the release of the last hold are not drawn here; see the snapshot lifecycle graph.
Bookmark destroy, channel-program destroys, `zfs destroy -p` output and the history and sysevent records are left out.
On a pool with a checkpoint, destroys free nothing until the checkpoint is discarded; this is not drawn.
Destroying an encryption root also destroys its key object and unloads its wrapping key (`dsl_dir_destroy_sync()`); zoned datasets are detached from their zone. Neither is drawn.
zpool destroy is drawn for an imported, healthy pool. Initialize, trim, rebuild and L2ARC rebuild stops, the ARC flush and log space map handling during unload are summarised.

page.title: ZFS Destroy Actions
page.intro: This diagram follows the destroy commands end to end: what `zfs destroy` does, and in what order, for a snapshot, a snapshot range, a file system or a volume (with `-r`, `-R`, `-f`, `-d`, `-n` and `-v`), what `zpool destroy` does to a pool, why each of them refuses (children, clones, holds, busy), and when the space actually comes back. The block-level freeing that a destroy starts (deadlists, the pool free list, the bptree, livelists) is drawn in detail in the snapshot lifecycle graph; this graph hands off to it.
